topic: Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, 2026

subtopics.title: Definition and Certification Changes
subtopics.summary: The Bill narrows the definition of transgender person and omits Section 4(2) of the 2019 Act, which had recognised a person's right to self-perceived gender identity. Identity would be verified by a Medical Board led by a Chief Medical Officer or Deputy CMO, and the District Magistrate would issue the certificate on the Board's recommendation. Individuals who undergo gender reassignment surgery must apply for a revised gender certificate.
facts: Bill omits Section 4(2) of the Transgender Persons Act, 2019.
Section 4(2) earlier recognised the right to self-perceived gender identity.
Definition keeps socio-cultural identities: Kinner, Hijra, Aravani, Jogta, Eunuch.

Removed categories: Trans-Man, Trans-Woman, Genderqueer.

District Magistrate issues certificate based on the Board's recommendation.
Gender reassignment surgery requires a revised gender certificate application.

subtopics.title: Penal, Reporting and National Council Provisions
subtopics.summary: The Bill expands penal provisions, with life imprisonment for forced mutilation of minors and up to 14 years for forcing children into begging. Medical institutions must report gender-affirming surgeries to the District Magistrate, and certificate holders can change their name in official documents. The National Council for Transgender Persons will include State and UT representatives, with rotational representation across regions.
facts: Life imprisonment for forced mutilation of minors.
Up to 14 years imprisonment for forcing children into begging.
Medical institutions must report gender-affirming surgeries to the District Magistrate.
Certificate holders can change their name in official documents.
National Council to include State and UT representatives.
Representation on the National Council is rotational across regions.
Council members must be of Director rank or above.
Council members are nominated by the Centre Govt.

subtopics.title: Significance and Criticism
subtopics.summary: Supporters say the narrower definition and medical certification target welfare, reduce the discretionary power of District Magistrates, and support a national healthcare database. Critics argue that removing self-identification contradicts the NALSA judgment, that medical verification may pathologise gender identity, and that surgery reporting may affect privacy. They also warn that broad terms could be used against NGOs and healthcare providers.
facts: Narrow definition aims to ensure benefits reach the most marginalised communities.
Medical Boards reduce the discretionary power of District Magistrates.
Mandatory reporting enables a national database for healthcare planning and welfare schemes.
Penal framework addresses mutilation, abduction and forced identity.
Removal of self-identification contradicts NALSA vs Union of India (2014).
NALSA judgment recognised gender identity as a Fundamental Right under Article 21.
Medical Board verification may pathologise gender identity.
Mandatory reporting of surgeries may violate medical confidentiality and personal privacy.
Broad terms like 'Inducement' or 'Allurement' could be used against NGOs and healthcare providers.
Such terms may restrict voluntary gender transition support.

subtopics.title: Legal and Welfare Background
subtopics.summary: Legal recognition of transgender persons in India developed through Supreme Court judgments and the 2019 Act. The NALSA judgment (2014) granted legal recognition and rights, and the 2019 Act provides legal recognition, protection of rights and welfare. Government initiatives include the SMILE scheme, a National Portal for ID cards and certificates, and Garima Greh shelter homes.
facts: NALSA vs Union of India (2014) granted legal recognition and rights to transgender persons.
Justice K.S. Puttaswamy vs Union of India (2017): Supreme Court ruled privacy a fundamental right.
Navtej Singh Johar vs Union of India (2018): Section 377 struck down, decriminalising same-sex relationships.
Transgender Persons Act, 2019 grants legal recognition and prohibits discrimination.
Supriyo vs Union of India (2023): a 5-Judge Constitution Bench rejected petitions to legalise same-sex marriage.
SMILE scheme provides comprehensive rehabilitation and medical cover for marginalised individuals.
National Portal lets transgender persons apply for ID cards and certificates without physical visits to offices.
Garima Greh: government shelter homes offering safe spaces, food and skill development for transgender persons in distress.

quizzes.passage: The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 was enacted after the Supreme Court's judgment in NALSA vs Union of India, which recognised transgender people as a third gender and granted them legal recognition and rights. The 2019 Act was passed to provide protection of rights of transgender persons and their welfare. The government has now presented the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, 2026 in the Lok Sabha to revise that Act. The Bill narrows the definition of transgender person and removes some categories, including trans-man, trans-woman and genderqueer. It also makes the penal framework stronger by expanding penal provisions. The offences it covers include forced mutilation of minors and the forcing of children into begging. The Bill requires medical institutions to report gender-affirming surgeries to an official authority. Under the Bill, certificate holders are allowed to change their name in official documents. The Bill further revises the composition of the National Council for Transgender Persons. The Bill's proposals have drawn both support and criticism, with critics pointing to the earlier Supreme Court judgment and supporters pointing to the aim of welfare. Its changes affect the penal, reporting and naming provisions of the law. These changes are discussed alongside the wider significance of the Bill.

quizzes.passage: The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 was passed to provide protection of rights of transgender persons and their welfare. The NALSA judgment in 2014 recognised transgender people as a third gender, and that recognition forms part of the background to the debate. The Union Government has now presented an Amendment Bill, 2026 in the Lok Sabha to revise that Act. The Bill narrows the definition of transgender person and makes the penal framework stronger by expanding penal provisions. Under the Bill, a Medical Board led by a Chief Medical Officer or Deputy CMO would verify transgender identity, and certificate holders could change their name in official documents. The Bill has drawn both support and criticism in public debate. Supporters argue that the Bill is meant to improve welfare for transgender persons. They also point out that mandatory reporting can support national planning for healthcare and welfare schemes. Critics question the Bill's approach and raise several concerns about it. They say that the verification process raises questions of its own. They also raise other concerns about the proposals, and they warn that some broad legal terms could be misused. The debate therefore covers welfare, certification, reporting and the wording of the law.

quizzes.passage: The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, 2026 has drawn both support and criticism. Supporters say the Bill aims to make welfare more targeted, and they point out that a narrower definition can help focus benefits. They also say that certification based on verification reduces the discretionary power of District Magistrates. According to supporters, mandatory reporting can help build a national record for planning healthcare and welfare schemes. They also note that the penal framework addresses serious crimes. Critics say that the Bill departs from an earlier Supreme Court judgment, which recognised rights for transgender persons. Critics also argue that the verification process raises concerns about how transgender people are assessed. They raise concerns about the reporting of certain procedures, and they warn that broad language in the Bill could be used against groups working in the sector. Such language, critics say, may also restrict support that people give voluntarily to those seeking transition-related help. The Bill also removes some categories from the definition of transgender person, and it changes the way such persons obtain certificates. The debate covers several parts of the Bill, including its penal, certification and reporting provisions. The Bill proposes changes to several parts of the law.
